title: FastAPI
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.
Bullets are keywords and flows, not explanations. If you need the explanation, you're in the wrong file — go to the note.
⭐ = the ones that decide the round. 🔥 = trending 2026. 📍 = you were actually asked this. 📝 = no vault note exists yet.
Trend-scanned: Aug 2026 · Depth: ⚠️ 14-fast-api/ is a stub (one unfinished index) — depth borrowed from 03-python/13-production-services/ · Bank: [[POPULAR-QUESTIONS]] · Scan: [[TREND-SCAN-2026-08]]

questions.text: What is ASGI, and why couldn't FastAPI be built on WSGI?
points: WSGI = one synchronous callable per request, blocking by construction
ASGI = async callable + scope / receive / send — long-lived connections possible
That's what unlocks WebSockets, SSE, streaming, lifespan
FastAPI is Starlette (ASGI) + Pydantic (validation); it isn't a server
Server is uvicorn/hypercorn — the app is just the callable
questions.flow: WSGI one blocking call → ASGI scope/receive/send → streams and sockets become possible
questions.trap: conflating FastAPI the framework with uvicorn the server

questions.text: How does FastAPI use type hints at runtime?
points: Introspects the function signature — annotations are the source of truth
Drives three things at once: validation · OpenAPI schema · dependency resolution
Annotated[T, Depends(...)] is the modern form — metadata rides with the type
This is why functools.wraps matters on decorators (see 01-PYTHON #11)
Same machinery emits JSON Schema → LLM tool definitions
questions.flow: signature introspected → validation + schema + DI all fall out of one declaration
questions.trap: treating hints as documentation — here they're executable

questions.text: Where does validation actually happen?
points: Request model parsed and coerced before your handler runs — body, query, path, headers
Failure → 422 with a structured error list, never reaching your code
Response model validates on the way out too (and filters — see #10)
Validate once at this boundary; the domain layer receives trusted objects
Custom validators / field_validator for cross-field invariants
questions.flow: parse → coerce → 422 on failure → typed object into handler → validated on the way out
questions.trap: re-validating inside the handler, paying twice

questions.text: def or async def for an endpoint — what changes?
points: async def → runs on the event loop; you must never block it
plain def → FastAPI runs it in a threadpool, so blocking is safe there
The dangerous combination is async def + a sync library
Threadpool is finite — sync endpoints cap out at pool size under load
Mixed codebase is fine; the choice is per-endpoint, not per-app
questions.flow: async def → loop, never block · def → threadpool, blocking OK · async + sync lib = the bug
questions.trap: async def everywhere "because it's faster", then calling requests inside

questions.text: What does Depends actually do?
points: Declares a callable whose result is injected; FastAPI resolves the graph per request
Dependencies can depend on dependencies — resolved as a DAG
Same dependency used twice in one request is cached by default (use_cache)
Can be sync or async; sync ones go to the threadpool like endpoints
Overridable in tests via app.dependency_overrides — the main testability win
questions.flow: declare callable → DAG resolved per request → cached within request → overridable in tests
questions.trap: describing it as a decorator or a middleware

questions.text: Path, query, body, header — how does FastAPI decide?
points: Name in the path template → path param
Scalar not in path → query param (default); Query(...) to be explicit
Pydantic model → body; multiple models → nested keys under field names
Header, Cookie, Form, File explicit; header names auto-convert _ → -
Annotated is the current idiom for all of these
questions.flow: in path → path · scalar → query · model → body · rest declared explicitly
questions.trap: a bare scalar you expected in the body silently becoming a query param

questions.text: Walk the request through the stack.
points: Middleware (outermost, sees raw request/response) → routing → dependencies → handler
Response unwinds back out through middleware in reverse
Exception handlers sit outside the handler, inside middleware
Middleware sees every request incl. 404; dependencies only matched routes
Ordering is registration order — auth before logging changes what gets logged
questions.flow: middleware → route match → dependency DAG → handler → response unwinds outward
questions.trap: putting per-route concerns in middleware and paying for them on every 404

questions.text: What's a yield dependency and when does teardown run?
points: Code before yield = setup, after = teardown — a context manager in DI form
Teardown runs after the response is generated, not when the handler returns
Right home for DB sessions, transactions, acquired clients
With StreamingResponse the ordering bites — see #14/#31
Exceptions: teardown still runs; you can catch around the yield
questions.flow: setup → yield value → handler → response → teardown
questions.trap: assuming teardown fires at handler return — it doesn't, and streams expose it

questions.text: Middleware, dependency, or exception handler — which for what?
points: Middleware — truly global, request/response shaped: CORS, tracing, timing, body size
Dependency — needs the DI graph or per-route config: auth, tenant resolution, DB session
Exception handler — maps a domain exception type to a response shape
Pure-ASGI middleware is cheaper than BaseHTTPMiddleware (which wraps in a task)
Prefer dependency when the concern varies per route
questions.flow: global + protocol-shaped → middleware · route-varying → dependency · error mapping → handler
questions.trap: BaseHTTPMiddleware for everything, then wondering where latency and context went

questions.text: What does response_model do beyond documentation?
points: Validates and filters the outgoing object to declared fields
That filtering is a security control — the standard way ORM objects leak password_hash
Handles serialisation: datetimes, enums, UUID, nested models
Costs a second validation pass — measurable on hot list endpoints
response_model_exclude_none / by_alias shape the wire contract
questions.flow: declare out-model → validate + filter → serialise → contract enforced in code
questions.trap: returning the ORM object directly and leaking columns you never listed

questions.text: BackgroundTasks — where does that run?
points: Runs after the response is sent, in the same process
Sync task → threadpool · async task → event loop
No durability: process dies → task is gone, no retry, no visibility
Fine for fire-and-forget side effects (audit log, cache warm, email)
Anything that must not be lost belongs on a real queue (see #18)
questions.flow: response sent → task runs in-process → no persistence, no retry
questions.trap: using it for payment, indexing, or anything you'd have to explain losing

questions.text: How do you turn a domain error into a good HTTP response?
points: HTTPException for the direct case; @app.exception_handler(Type) for domain errors
Handler keeps HTTP concerns out of the domain layer — domain raises its own exception type
RequestValidationError → 422 by default; override to reshape the payload
Return a consistent error envelope (code, message, correlation ID) — clients parse it
Never leak stack traces or internal identifiers
questions.flow: domain raises domain error → registered handler maps to status + envelope + correlation ID
questions.trap: HTTPException deep in the service layer, coupling domain to HTTP

questions.text: Where do you load the model / open the pool?
points: lifespan async context manager — startup before serving, shutdown after draining
Load once per worker process; N workers → N copies in memory (see #16)
Hold handles in app.state, not module globals, so tests can swap them
Warm-up call in lifespan avoids the first request paying compile/JIT cost
Shutdown side must close pools and cancel background tasks
questions.flow: lifespan startup → load + warm → serve → shutdown drains and closes
questions.trap: lazy-loading on first request — the cold start lands on a real user

questions.text: Stream LLM tokens out of FastAPI. Show me the shape.
points: StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream"), chunks as data: {...}\n\n
Async generator pulls from the provider and yields — never buffer the whole answer
Disable proxy buffering or nothing ships until completion
Client disconnect must cancel upstream — otherwise you pay for unread tokens
Errors after headers are sent → in-band error event, not a 500
questions.flow: async gen → SSE frames → unbuffered proxy → cancel upstream on disconnect
questions.trap: yield-ing from inside a yield dependency's session and having it close mid-stream

questions.text: Where does the OpenAPI schema come from?
points: Generated from routes + type hints + Pydantic models — no separate spec file
response_model, status codes, tags, summary/description all feed it
Consequence: the schema is only as good as your annotations
Can be exported for client codegen and contract tests
Lock it in CI — an unnoticed schema diff is a broken client
questions.flow: routes + hints + models → schema → export → codegen and contract test
questions.trap: hand-maintaining API docs beside a schema that already generates itself

questions.text: uvicorn or gunicorn? How many workers?
points: uvicorn alone is fine in a container where the orchestrator does process supervision
gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker when you want a process manager in-pod
Starting point ~2×CPU+1 for generic web — but that heuristic is wrong for AI services
Real ceiling is memory × workers when each loads a model or big cache
Async I/O-bound → fewer workers, high concurrency each; don't scale workers to fix a blocked loop
questions.flow: container supervises → uvicorn · need in-pod manager → gunicorn → then size by memory, not CPU
questions.trap: quoting 2×CPU+1 for a service holding a model per worker

questions.text: When is a plain def endpoint the better choice?
points: When the work is genuinely sync and the library has no async story (many SDKs, some drivers)
Threadpool isolates the blocking — safer than a half-async wrapper you got wrong
Also fine for short CPU work that would otherwise stall the loop
Ceiling: threadpool size (tunable) — beyond that requests queue
Don't mix: async def calling a sync client is worse than either pure option
questions.flow: no async client available → sync def → threadpool absorbs it → watch pool size
questions.trap: wrapping sync calls in async def without an executor and calling it async

questions.text: BackgroundTasks or a real queue?
points: BackgroundTasks: zero infra, zero durability — dies with the process
Queue: persistence, retries, DLQ, backpressure, independent scaling, observability
Decision axis: can you explain losing this to a customer?
Also queue when the work outlives a deploy or needs its own resource profile (GPU)
Middle ground: enqueue from a background task if the response must not wait
questions.flow: can it be lost? → yes → BackgroundTasks · no → queue with retry + DLQ
questions.trap: document indexing or embedding in BackgroundTasks — silently lost on redeploy

questions.text: Auth as middleware or as a dependency?
points: Dependency — per-route, composable, appears in OpenAPI, overridable in tests, returns typed principal
Middleware — blanket enforcement, catches unmatched routes, good for a hard deny-by-default
JWT verification: signature + exp + aud/iss; cache JWKS, don't fetch per request
Authorisation (can this tenant touch this row) belongs in the domain, not the edge
Common shape: middleware for deny-by-default, dependency for identity + scopes
questions.flow: identity/scopes → dependency · blanket deny → middleware · row-level authz → domain
questions.trap: stopping at authentication and calling it authorisation

questions.text: response_model is costing you p99. Now what?
points: It's a second full validation pass — visible on large list responses
Options: narrower response models, pagination, model_construct on trusted internal paths
Or return a pre-serialised payload and document the schema manually — you're trading safety
Measure first: often the serialiser isn't the cost, the N+1 behind it is
Keep it on any endpoint returning ORM-backed objects — the leak risk outweighs the ms
questions.flow: measure → narrow the model / paginate → only then consider skipping validation
questions.trap: removing response_model on a user-facing endpoint and reopening the field-leak hole

questions.text: Sync SQLAlchemy in the threadpool, or the async engine?
points: Async engine: true non-blocking, but lazy loading is a trap — must eager-load explicitly
Sync in threadpool: mature, simpler, all patterns work; capped by pool size
Session must be request-scoped — a yield dependency is the natural home
Pool sizing is per process, so real DB connections = pool × workers × replicas (01-PYTHON #30)
Transaction should be narrower than the request; never hold across an LLM call
questions.flow: async engine + eager loads · or sync + threadpool → request-scoped session → narrow transaction
questions.trap: holding a DB transaction open across a multi-second model call

questions.text: Why FastAPI and not Flask / Django / Litestar?
points: FastAPI: async-native, schema-from-types, strong ecosystem — the default for AI backends
Django wins when you want ORM + admin + auth + migrations as one opinionated whole
Flask for tiny sync services; async story is bolted on
Litestar — similar model, more batteries, smaller community
Honest framing: choose by team and what else the service needs, not benchmarks
questions.flow: async + schema-driven → FastAPI · full batteries → Django · tiny sync → Flask
questions.trap: citing benchmark numbers as the reason

questions.text: How do you lay out a FastAPI service that's going to grow?
points: Layers: api/ (routers, schemas) · domain/ (entities, services, ports) · infrastructure/ (DB, clients, adapters)
Dependency direction points inward — domain imports nothing from api or infra
APIRouter per bounded context, mounted with prefix and tags
DI wires adapters at the edge, so swapping a provider is one binding
Rule: if it imports fastapi, it isn't domain code
questions.flow: api → domain ← infrastructure → dependencies point inward → routers per context
questions.trap: foldering by type (models/, views/) — the coupling survives the rename

questions.text: Where does config live?
points: pydantic-settings BaseSettings — env vars validated and typed at startup
Fail fast on missing/invalid config; never discover it on first request
Secrets from the platform (env, secret manager), never in the repo or image
One settings object, injected as a cached dependency — not read ad hoc
Per-environment overrides by env var, not by branching in code
questions.flow: env → typed Settings → validated at startup → injected once
questions.trap: os.getenv scattered through modules with silent None defaults

questions.text: How do you test it?
points: TestClient (sync) or httpx.AsyncClient + ASGITransport for async — no network, no server
app.dependency_overrides to swap DB/LLM/auth — the main reason to use DI at all
Real DB in a container for repository tests; mocks for provider calls
Deterministic LLM tests need recorded or stubbed responses — never live calls in CI
Contract-test the OpenAPI schema so client breakage fails the build
questions.flow: ASGI transport → override deps → real DB for repos, stubs for providers → schema contract test
questions.trap: mocking so deep the test only proves the mock works

questions.text: Client asks for a breaking change. How do you version?
points: URL path versioning (/v1, /v2) — blunt, obvious, easy to route and observe
Additive changes don't need a version; removals and semantic changes do
Run both versions off one domain layer; version the schema, not the logic
Deprecation needs a date, a header, and usage metrics — or nothing migrates
Generated OpenAPI diff in CI tells you when you broke it by accident
questions.flow: additive → no version · breaking → /v2 on shared domain → deprecate with data and a date
questions.trap: versioning the whole service and forking business logic

questions.text: Rate limiting and quotas — where?
points: Edge (gateway/ingress) for crude abuse; in-app for per-tenant, per-feature, token-aware limits
LLM endpoints need token budgets, not just request counts — cost isn't per call
Shared counter (Redis, atomic) or per-process limiters multiply by worker count
Return 429 + Retry-After; decide fail-open vs fail-closed if Redis is down
Quota (monthly spend) is a different mechanism from rate limit (burst) — don't conflate
questions.flow: gateway for abuse → in-app per-tenant token budget → shared atomic counter → 429 + Retry-After
questions.trap: counting requests on an endpoint where one request can cost 100×another

questions.text: p99 tripled, CPU is flat. Go.
points: Flat CPU + rising latency = waiting, not computing
Candidates: blocked event loop · connection-pool checkout queue · exhausted threadpool · slow upstream
py-spy dump on a live worker shows exactly where it's parked
Check pool wait time and threadpool saturation as first-class metrics, not just endpoint latency
Upstream provider latency needs its own timeout + breaker or it becomes your latency
questions.flow: flat CPU → it's a wait → py-spy the worker → loop / pool / threadpool / upstream
questions.trap: scaling replicas, which multiplies pool pressure and makes it worse

questions.text: How do you call an upstream provider properly?
points: One shared httpx.AsyncClient for the app lifetime — per-request clients kill connection reuse
Create in lifespan, close on shutdown
Explicit timeouts: connect / read / write / pool — never rely on defaults
Retry only idempotent calls, bounded, with jitter; add a circuit breaker
Streaming calls need their own longer read timeout, not the global one
questions.flow: shared client in lifespan → explicit timeouts → bounded jittered retry → breaker
questions.trap: a new AsyncClient per request — TLS handshake on every call

questions.text: Pod gets SIGTERM mid-stream. What should happen?
points: Stop accepting new connections, drain in-flight, then exit
lifespan shutdown must close pools and cancel background tasks
Long streams may exceed the grace period → cap stream duration deliberately
Readiness probe should fail before shutdown starts so traffic drains first
Client needs a resume story (event IDs) or the user just sees a truncated answer
questions.flow: fail readiness → stop accepting → drain → close pools → exit within grace
questions.trap: grace period shorter than your longest stream, so every deploy cuts users off

questions.text: Someone uploads a 2 GB PDF.
points: UploadFile spools to disk past a threshold — but a naive .read() still loads it all
Stream to storage/parse in chunks; never materialise the whole body
Enforce a max size at the proxy and in-app — client-declared length is untrusted
Validate content type by sniffing, not the header
Heavy parsing goes to a worker; the endpoint returns a job handle (see #18)
questions.flow: size cap at edge → stream chunks → sniff type → hand off to worker → return job id
questions.trap: await file.read() and an OOMKill under concurrent uploads

questions.text: WebSockets across multiple workers — what breaks?
points: Connections are pinned to one worker/pod — in-memory rooms don't span replicas
Need a shared broker (Redis pub/sub, etc.) to fan out across processes
Sticky sessions or a connection-aware LB; plain round-robin breaks reconnect
Heartbeats + explicit close codes; idle proxies kill silent connections
Backpressure per socket — a slow consumer must not grow an unbounded buffer
questions.flow: per-worker pinning → shared broker for fan-out → heartbeat → per-socket backpressure
questions.trap: an in-memory connections dict that works on one replica and fails on two

questions.text: Liveness and readiness for a service that loads a 5 GB model.
points: Liveness = am I wedged (restart me) · Readiness = can I serve now (route to me)
Model load can take minutes → readiness must stay false until warm, or use a startup probe
Liveness must not depend on downstream DB/provider — that turns a partial outage into a restart storm
Readiness may consider critical deps, deliberately
Probe timeouts under load are a classic self-inflicted restart loop
questions.flow: startup probe for load → readiness gates traffic → liveness stays dependency-free
questions.trap: one /health wired to both, checking the DB — DB blip becomes a cluster-wide restart

questions.text: It works locally, breaks behind the ingress.
points: Proxy buffering — SSE/streaming arrives all at once at the end
CORS: preflight, credentials, and the fact that * + credentials is invalid
X-Forwarded-* / --proxy-headers or every client IP looks like the proxy
Idle and read timeouts at the LB shorter than your longest request
Request/body size limits enforced upstream, returning a shape your client can't parse
questions.flow: buffering → CORS → forwarded headers → LB timeouts → size limits
questions.trap: debugging the app for hours on something the ingress config caused

questions.text: Design the FastAPI layer of a RAG service.
points: Edge: authn → tenant resolution → token-aware rate limit → validation → idempotency key
/query streams (SSE); /ingest returns a job handle, work goes to a queue
Lifespan loads embedding model + opens vector-store and DB pools once per worker
Retrieval and generation get separate timeouts and breakers — they fail differently
Response carries citations and a request ID; both are contract, not decoration
questions.flow: authn → tenant → budget → validate → stream query ‖ enqueue ingest → cite + correlate
questions.trap: one synchronous endpoint doing ingest and query, sharing a timeout

questions.text: Multi-tenant. How do you keep tenants apart?
points: Tenant resolved once at the edge into a request-scoped context, never from a client-supplied body field
Isolation ladder: shared table + row filter → schema-per-tenant → database-per-tenant
Vector store needs the same story — namespace/filter per tenant, enforced server-side
Per-tenant quotas, budgets and metrics; noisy-neighbour is the real failure mode
Every log and span carries tenant ID — otherwise incidents aren't attributable
questions.flow: resolve tenant at edge → context → enforced filter in repo + vector store → per-tenant budget
questions.trap: trusting a tenant_id in the request body; filtering in the service layer instead of the repository

questions.text: An agent run takes four minutes. Request/response doesn't fit.
points: Switch to job semantics: POST → 202 + job id → poll or subscribe
Stream intermediate steps (SSE/WS) so the user sees progress, not a spinner
Persist run state so a disconnect or redeploy doesn't lose it
Cancellation must be a real endpoint that propagates to the worker
Bound it: step cap, wall-clock cap, token budget — see [[TREND-SCAN-2026-08]]
questions.flow: 202 + job id → worker executes → stream steps → persist state → cancellable → hard caps
questions.trap: a long-poll HTTP request holding a worker and dying at the LB timeout

questions.text: What's the contract with the frontend for a streaming answer?
points: Typed event kinds, not raw text: token · tool_call · citation · done · error
Errors after headers are in-band events — the status code is already 200
Include a request/trace ID in the first event for support and debugging
Sequence numbers or event IDs so a client can detect gaps and resume
Define what a partial answer means — is a truncated response billable, retryable, cacheable?
questions.flow: typed events → in-band errors → trace id first → sequence for resume → define partial
questions.trap: streaming bare text, leaving the client to regex out errors and citations

questions.text: What do you put on the dashboard for an LLM endpoint?
points: TTFT and inter-token latency — total duration hides the felt experience
Tokens in/out and cost, sliced per tenant and per feature
Upstream provider error and rate-limit counts, separated from your own 5xx
Model + prompt version on every span, or regressions can't be attributed
Saturation signals: pool wait, threadpool queue, event-loop lag
questions.flow: TTFT → cost per tenant → provider errors split out → version tags → saturation
questions.trap: a dashboard of RPS and 5xx that stays green while quality and spend degrade

questions.text: Tell me about a FastAPI service you had to restructure or rescue.
points: Open with what it cost — change risk, test time, an incident, onboarding drag
The structural diagnosis: what was importing what it shouldn't
The move: api/ · domain/ · infrastructure/, dependencies pointing inward
What you deliberately didn't do — big-bang rewrite, framework swap
Number: <fill> — see [[War-Stories]] #4, this Result is still blank
questions.flow: cost in business terms → structural diagnosis → incremental move → what you refused → number
questions.trap: "it was cleaner afterwards" with nothing measured
